newsitem.title: USA: Dollar ends mostly lower in U.S., Canadian dlr up.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends mostly lower in U.S., Canadian dlr up.

text.p: The dollar fell against the Canadian dollar after the Bank of Canada surprised investors by raising official interest rates, dealers said. The dollar edged lower against most other currencies, notably the yen.
The Bank of Canada intervened in the market Thursday to raise its key bank rate to 3.5 percent from 3.25, triggering heavy selling of U.S. dollars for Canadian paper.

"That took everyone by surprise. There was a lot of liquidation of long U.S. dollar positions and some establishment of short U.S. dollar positions," said Seth Garrett, chief dealer at Credit Suiss First Boston.
The dollar got as low as Canadian $1.3770 during the session, and ended lower at C$1.3818/23 at Thursday's close from C$1.3954/59 at the open.
The greenback dipped to 1.7250/60 marks from 1.7260/70 and fell to 113.10/20 yen from 113.50/60.
Traders marveled at the Bank of Canada's bold move, which clearly had not been expected in the market.
"You don't get a 200-point move when it's expected. The magnitude of that move tells you the market was unprepared," said Bruce Giammattei, senior trader at Mellon Bank.

Bundesbank council member Reimut Jochimsen triggered modest dollar buying in European trading when he told an audience in Frankfurt he could not rule out a cut in interest rates, even though he did not see one on the horizon.
"You couldn't really say the dollar was strong, but nobody was wild about buying German marks," said Giammattei.
But by the end of the session, the greenback had settled into a narrow range, unable to break through 1.73 marks, where European central banks were reportedly waiting with dollar offers.
The mark fell nearly a full yen to 65.55 yen on the day, which helped keep a lid on dollar/yen as well, dealers said.
"The dollar got sold down pretty convincingly against the yen," Giammattei said.
Dealers had expected technical support to hold at 113.50, but the dollar easily fell through and found backup support near 113.

The dollar rose against the French franc overnight after news that French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin instructed his ministers to focus on job creation and not necessarily reducing the federal budget deficit in the year ahead.
Investors have serious questions about France's ability to meet the deficit target to qualify for proposed European monetary union (EMU) in 1999, and the French franc was sold on the news.
"The only reason I can think of to own the French franc is that it might be part of EMU. Should EMU fail, the French franc would suffer a great deal," Giammattei said.

Also hurting the franc was a report in a French magazine that Bank of France monetary policy committee member Jean-Pierre Gerard said he would prefer to see the dollar rise to 6.20 francs from its current level.
But the dollar slipped back in U.S. trade amid profit-taking, dealers noted.
The greenback ended at 5.8200/30 French francs, down from 5.8255/85.
The British pound dipped to $1.6652/62 from $1.6663/70. The dollar fell to 1.4355/65 Swiss francs from 1.4380/90. The Australian dollar was virtually unchanged at $0.7501/06.
((--Chris Stetkiewicz, 212-859-1664))
